items.fix: Add a clearly explained, optional choice: "Send all future letters and documents to me in this format". Record it as a communication preference on the contact record, not as a diagnosis, and use it for every outgoing letter. Say how to change or remove it.
items.impact: A constant, repeated barrier. Every letter is late in a usable form, so the risk of missed deadlines returns with every letter. People must keep relying on others to read their private mail.
items.problem: The form asks the tenant to name one item ("What do you need in another format?") each time. Nothing lets them say "send me all future letters in this format". Every new rent statement, repair appointment or notice arrives first in standard print, and the tenant must notice it, get someone to read it, and ask again. The form has a single free-text item field (line 140) and no preference or "all future letters" option. Affects blind and partially sighted tenants, Braille and audio users, people needing Easy Read, and Deaf BSL users.
items.where: statement.html, form lines 109 to 143; line 108 "If you need a letter, form or page in a different format, fill in this form"

items.fix: Add a "Check your answers" page with "Change" links for each answer, then a confirmation page with a reference number, expected delivery date and contact route, also sent in the format the person asked for. Test the full submit journey with screen reader users and people with learning disabilities.
items.impact: Wrong or unintended disclosures cannot be caught. Users do not know whether the request was received, so they ask again or give up.
items.problem: A single press of "Send request" submits health information that, by the page's own account, goes to the housing officer and the tenancy file. There is no "Check your answers" page, no way to review or correct entries, and nothing says what happens after submission (confirmation, reference number, email receipt). The page claims the highest conformance level, which requires submissions to be reversible, checked or confirmed; even at the middle level a review step is best practice for sensitive data. It is one submit button posting straight to `/accessibility/request`. Affects people with cognitive disabilities, memory difficulties or tremor, screen reader users, and anyone who chose the wrong option by mistake.

items.fix: Open with plain-language sentences, for example "Most of this website should work with screen readers, keyboard only and zoom. These parts do not work well yet: ...". Expand "Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG)" on first use and explain the level in one sentence. Offer an Easy Read version. Check understanding with tenants with learning disabilities.
items.impact: Users cannot tell what the statement means for them, which is the whole purpose of the page.
items.problem: The badge "WCAG 2.3 AAA verified" is the first thing read after the h1. "WCAG" is expanded only in the next paragraph, and "Level AAA", "conformant" and "automated accessibility audits" are never explained. The audience is tenants, not web professionals. The page claims the highest level, so rules on unusual words, abbreviations and reading level also apply. No definitions appear on the page. Affects people with learning disabilities, low literacy or cognitive impairment, and screen reader users who hear "W C A G 2.3 triple A verified" with no context.
items.where: statement.html, badge on line 98 and paragraph on line 101

items.fix: Set `max-width: 70ch` (or about 38rem) on the text container, and keep the highest-level claim out of the statement until each criterion has been tested.
items.impact: Slower, more tiring reading and losing the start of the next line.
items.problem: 46rem is about 736px at the default size. Arial at 16px averages about half an em per character, so a full line runs to about 85 to 90 characters after padding. The highest conformance level asks for no more than 80 characters per line. Minor in itself, but one of several facts showing the "fully conformant at Level AAA" claim is untrue. Affects people with dyslexia, low vision and attention difficulties, who lose their place on long lines.

items.fix: Add a first paragraph naming the website, the services and subdomains in scope and those excluded, as in the model accessibility statement.
items.impact: Users cannot tell whether the claims apply to the parts they need, and meet barriers in parts the statement silently leaves out.
items.problem: There is no scope sentence, such as "This statement applies to the Greyfield Homes tenant website at [address], including the tenant portal, online rent payments and repair reporting". "Every page" and "any page" (lines 101 and 102) are not defined, and third-party parts (payment provider, repairs booking system, PDF letters, any mobile app) are not mentioned. No scope text appears anywhere. Affects disabled tenants deciding whether to use the site for payments or repairs, and advocates helping them.
